material_status: fictional AI-assisted development examples; not administered or independently validated

tasks.title: School exhibition plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints

tasks.claim: Plan C is the plan to choose under the stated rule.

correct.reason: Contradicted. Plan C has the largest seat count, but its cost exceeds the stated budget. The rule permits comparison only among plans meeting both requirements. Plan A meets those requirements and is the eligible choice.

misleading.reason: Supported. Plan C has the largest seat count, so it provides the most exhibition places. The stated priority is to maximize seats. Since C reaches the minimum number of seats, it is the plan to choose.

tasks.shared_feedback: Contradicted. C costs 108, above the budget of 100. B has only 18 seats, below the minimum of 20. A meets both constraints. The priority applies only after checking eligibility.
tasks.learning_skill: Check constraints before applying a stated objective
tasks.development_concern: Budget and seating are invented task rules, not a definition of what a school ought to value.

tasks.title: School newsletter workshops
tasks.claim: A larger proportion of invited students completed the workshop in Group A.

correct.reason: Supported. Group A has 24 completions among 60 invited students, while Group B has 35 among 100. The question asks about completion proportions. Dividing each count by its own invitation total gives A the higher proportion.

misleading.reason: Contradicted. Group A has 24 completions while Group B has 35 completions. The question compares workshop completion, and B has the larger completion total. That larger total shows B has the higher completion proportion among invited students.

tasks.shared_feedback: Supported. A has 24/60 = 40%; B has 35/100 = 35%. B has more completers, but A has the higher proportion among invited students.
tasks.learning_skill: Choose the denominator corresponding to the claim
tasks.development_concern: May test prior arithmetic knowledge; pretest whether feedback supports learning rather than ceiling performance.

tasks.title: Two school club activity days
tasks.claim: Across both days together, 35% of students completed all stations.

correct.reason: Contradicted. The two days have unequal numbers of students. The combined completion proportion uses total completions divided by total students. There are 33 completers out of 120 students, so the pooled percentage is 27.5 rather than 35.

misleading.reason: Supported. The small day has a 50% completion proportion and the large day has a 20% completion proportion. Averaging these two percentages gives 35%. This average is the completion proportion across the two school activity days together.

tasks.shared_feedback: Contradicted. Combine counts: (15 + 18)/(30 + 90) = 33/120 = 27.5%. The mean of day percentages weights the smaller day equally and answers a different question.
tasks.development_concern: Decimal calculation may add burden; adjust numbers after educator review without silently altering the scoring key.

tasks.title: Classroom recycling project
tasks.claim: The new recycling project caused the entire decrease in paper waste.

correct.reason: Not enough information. Paper waste was lower in the later week, but the record has no comparison group or account of other changes. It establishes a decrease. It does not isolate how much of that decrease the recycling project caused.

misleading.reason: Supported. Paper waste fell after the recycling project began in the same class. The record shows a decrease of 30 sheets, so this difference measures the effect of the project. The project caused the entire recorded decrease in waste.

tasks.shared_feedback: Not enough information. Waste decreased by 30 sheets. Without evidence ruling out other influences, this record cannot establish that the project caused the entire decrease. It also does not establish zero effect.
tasks.learning_skill: Distinguish an observed change from an isolated causal effect
tasks.development_concern: A plausible alternative explanation and a clearly bounded claim need human review; do not reward reflexive skepticism.

tasks.title: School reading room plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints

tasks.claim: Plan B is the plan to choose under the stated rule.

correct.reason: Supported. Plan B stays within the budget and provides at least the required number of seats. Plan A costs too much, and Plan C has too few seats. B is the only eligible plan under the stated decision rule.

misleading.reason: Contradicted. Plan A offers more seats than Plan B and therefore best meets the priority of maximizing seating. Both A and B exceed the required minimum number of seats. The plan with the larger seating total is the one to choose.

tasks.shared_feedback: Supported. B costs 86, within the budget of 90, and has 22 seats, at least 16. A fails the budget requirement and C fails the seating requirement.
tasks.learning_skill: Apply the same constraint rule to new figures
tasks.development_concern: The example deliberately changes the correct label and winning plan; this does not establish equal difficulty across forms.

tasks.title: School planting sessions
tasks.claim: A larger proportion of invited students completed the session in Group X.

correct.reason: Contradicted. Group X has more completers, but it also invited more students. The relevant proportions are 32 out of 80 and 25 out of 50. Comparing those proportions gives Y, rather than X, the higher completion proportion.

misleading.reason: Supported. Group X has 32 completers, compared with 25 in Group Y. The question asks which session achieved more completion, and X has the larger recorded total. That larger completion total shows X had the higher proportion among invited students.

tasks.shared_feedback: Contradicted. X has 32/80 = 40%, while Y has 25/50 = 50%. More completers does not establish a higher completion proportion.
tasks.learning_skill: Apply denominator choice to a new setting
tasks.development_concern: A related new task measures near transfer, not broad independent judgment or real-world decision quality.

tasks.title: Two school library activity days
tasks.claim: Across both days together, 50% of students completed all activities.

correct.reason: Supported. The combined proportion uses total completions divided by total students. There are 12 plus 48 completions among 40 plus 80 students. The resulting 60 out of 120 is 50%, matching the claim about both days together.

misleading.reason: Contradicted. The small day has a 30% completion proportion and the large day has a 60% completion proportion. Averaging these percentages gives 45%. That is the combined completion proportion, so the claim that half of students completed is false.

tasks.shared_feedback: Supported. (12 + 48)/(40 + 80) = 60/120 = 50%. The 45% mean weights days equally, rather than weighting each student equally.
tasks.learning_skill: Pool unequal groups with new numbers
tasks.development_concern: The phrase across both days must be understood consistently; no real school events are represented.

tasks.title: School art project display
tasks.claim: Changing the display caused the entire increase in average visitors.

correct.reason: Not enough information. Average visitors increased after the display changed, but the record gives no comparison group or information about other changes. The increase is observed. The share of the increase caused by the display change is not established.

misleading.reason: Supported. Average visitors increased from 40 to 55 after the display changed in the same room. This before-and-after difference is 15 visitors, so it measures the effect of changing the display. The changed display caused the entire recorded increase.

tasks.shared_feedback: Not enough information. An increase of 15 visitors was observed. The record does not separate the display change from other possible influences and does not establish that it had no effect.
tasks.learning_skill: Transfer the distinction between observed change and cause
tasks.development_concern: Same answer category as its practice counterpart could cue memorization; expand and balance the full bank.

tasks.title: School poster workshops
tasks.claim: A larger proportion of invited students completed the workshop in Group A.

correct.reason: Contradicted. Group A has 20 completions among 40 invited students, while Group B has 36 among 60. The question asks about completion proportions. Dividing each completion count by its invitation total gives B the higher proportion.

misleading.reason: Supported. Group A has 20 invited students who did not complete, while Group B has 24. The question compares workshop completion. Because A has fewer students who did not complete, it has the higher completion proportion among invited students.

tasks.shared_feedback: Contradicted. A has 20/40 = 50%; B has 36/60 = 60%. A has fewer non-completers (20 versus 24), but those counts have different invitation totals. Fewer non-completers does not establish a higher completion proportion.
tasks.learning_skill: Choose the denominator corresponding to the claim
tasks.misleading_error: Compares non-completion counts without their invitation totals.
tasks.explanation_anchor: A: 20/40 = 50%; B: 36/60 = 60%; A is not the larger proportion. Equivalent fractions or a valid cross-product are acceptable.
tasks.development_concern: This uses non-completion counts, unlike Y02. Similar length does not establish equal difficulty or advice plausibility.

tasks.title: School bookmark workshops

record.note: Every completer was invited. Group A's invitation total was not recorded; unknown is not zero.

tasks.claim: A larger proportion of invited students completed the workshop in Group A.

correct.reason: Not enough information. Group B has 30 completions among 60 invited students, but Group A has 24 completions with no invitation total recorded. The question asks about proportions among invitees. Without that total, the record cannot establish which proportion is larger.

misleading.reason: Contradicted. Group A has 24 completions while Group B has 30 completions. The question compares workshop completion. Group B achieved the larger completion count, so its completion proportion is higher. The recorded counts therefore contradict the claim about Group A.

tasks.shared_feedback: Not enough information. B has 30/60 = 50%, but A's invitation total is unknown. If A had 40 invitees, 24/40 = 60%; if it had 80, 24/80 = 30%. Both hypothetical totals fit the record and imply opposite rankings. These are examples, not extra observed facts.
tasks.learning_skill: Identify when the denominator required by a claim is unavailable
tasks.misleading_error: Infers a proportion ordering from completion counts when one denominator is absent.
tasks.explanation_anchor: B is 50%, but A cannot be compared without its invitation total. A correct explanation identifies the missing denominator and its consequence; it need not invent numerical scenarios.
tasks.development_concern: The visibly missing value may cue the answer. Only one rates practice item has missing data; the full bank must avoid a universal surface rule.

tasks.learning_skill: Check whether missing information can change the choice under the supplied constraints
tasks.title: School science display plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints

record.note: B's seat count was not recorded. All costs and seat counts are non-negative whole numbers; an unknown value is not zero.

tasks.claim: Plan A is the plan to choose under the stated rule.

correct.reason: Supported. Plan B costs more than the budget, so it is excluded whatever its missing seat count might be. Plans A and C meet both requirements. A has 26 seats and C has 22, so A is the eligible choice with more seats.

misleading.reason: Not enough information. Plan B's seat count was not recorded, and the priority is to select the plan with the most seats. Without knowing B's seat count, we cannot compare all three plans or establish that A has the largest number of seats.

tasks.shared_feedback: Supported. B costs 128, above the budget of 100, so its missing seat count cannot make it eligible. A costs 94 and has 26 seats; C costs 82 and has 22 seats. Both meet the requirements, and A has more seats. The missing value cannot change this choice.

answer_basis.logical_reason: B is ineligible because its known cost exceeds the budget; varying its seats cannot change that exclusion.

tasks.misleading_error: Treats an unknown seat count as relevant despite the known budget exclusion.
tasks.explanation_anchor: B already fails the budget, so its unknown seats cannot affect eligibility. A and C qualify; A's 26 seats exceed C's 22. A numerical guess for B is neither required nor justified.
tasks.development_concern: Missingness appears in B's seat count and the answer remains Supported. One case breaks a blanket missing-means-unknown shortcut but does not remove field-position or variable-type cues.

tasks.learning_skill: Check whether missing information can change the choice under the supplied constraints
tasks.title: School history display plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints

record.note: B's cost was not recorded. All costs and seat counts are non-negative whole numbers; an unknown value is not zero.

tasks.claim: Plan B is the plan to choose under the stated rule.

correct.reason: Not enough information. B has more seats than A or C, but its cost was not recorded. The choice must meet the budget as well as the seat requirement. If B is within budget it wins; if it exceeds budget it is excluded and A wins.

misleading.reason: Supported. Plan B has 30 seats, compared with 26 for A and 22 for C. The priority is to choose the plan with the largest seat count. B also exceeds the required minimum of 20 seats, so its highest seating total makes it the plan to choose.

tasks.shared_feedback: Not enough information. If B costs 96, it meets the budget and its 30 seats make it the choice. If B costs 108, it exceeds the budget and A is the choice with 26 seats. Both hypothetical costs fit the supplied record. They show why B's missing cost matters; neither is an observed value.

answer_basis.logical_reason: Compatible values of B's unreported cost lead to different eligible winners and opposite truth values for the claim.

tasks.misleading_error: Uses the largest seat count without establishing that B satisfies the budget constraint.
tasks.explanation_anchor: B's unknown cost could lie within or above the budget. That changes its eligibility and whether it beats A. Identifying the decisive cost uncertainty is sufficient; numeric counterexamples are optional.
tasks.development_concern: The unknown cost matters here, whereas unknown seats do not matter in Y11. Cost-versus-seats, B's position and repeated tables can themselves become cues; current three-item family does not establish equal difficulty.

tasks.learning_skill: Check whether missing information can change the choice under the supplied constraints
tasks.title: School language display plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints
requirements.tie_break: Lower cost when seat counts tie

record.note: C's seat count was not recorded. All costs and seat counts are non-negative whole numbers; an unknown value is not zero. If eligible plans have the same seat count, choose the lower-cost plan.

tasks.claim: Plan C is the plan to choose under the stated rule.

correct.reason: Not enough information. C is within budget, but its seat count is unknown. It could fail the minimum or seat fewer people than A; it could also seat more. The stated tie rule settles an equal count, but it cannot supply C's unrecorded count.

misleading.reason: Supported. C costs 90, within the budget of 100, and costs less than A. The rule favors the lower-cost plan when comparing equal seating, so C offers the better choice. Its missing seat count does not change its known cost advantage over A.

tasks.shared_feedback: Not enough information. If C has 18 seats, it fails the minimum and A wins with 24. If C has 28 seats, C qualifies and wins. At 24 seats, C wins the tie because it costs less than A. These are possible completions, not recorded seat counts; C's missing seats can change the answer.

answer_basis.logical_reason: Compatible seat counts leave C ineligible or make it the winner. A lower known cost alone does not establish the largest eligible seat count.

tasks.misleading_error: Applies the lower-cost tie rule without establishing equal seat counts, and treats the unknown seats as irrelevant.
tasks.explanation_anchor: C's missing seats could change its eligibility or its rank against A. For equal seats the supplied lower-cost rule applies; cost alone does not settle the choice. Numerical scenarios are optional.
tasks.development_concern: A decisive missing-seat case reverses the Y11 field-type shortcut. C position, target wording, an explicit tie rule and label patterns remain potential cues; no matched difficulty or age suitability is established.

tasks.title: School music display plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints
requirements.tie_break: Lower cost when seat counts tie

record.note: C's cost was not recorded. All costs and seat counts are non-negative whole numbers; an unknown value is not zero. If eligible plans have the same seat count, choose the lower-cost plan.

tasks.claim: Plan A is the plan to choose under the stated rule.

correct.reason: Supported. C has only 18 seats, below the required minimum, so its missing cost cannot make it eligible. A and B both meet the budget and seat requirements. A has 24 seats compared with B's 22, making A the choice under the stated rule.

misleading.reason: Not enough information. C's cost is unknown, and the rule includes a budget limit and a preference for lower cost when seats tie. Without this cost, the comparison is incomplete. C could be cheaper than A, so the record cannot establish that A is the plan to choose.

tasks.shared_feedback: Supported. C has 18 seats, below the minimum of 20, whatever its cost might be. A costs 96 and has 24 seats; B costs 82 and has 22 seats. Both qualify, and A has more seats. There is no tie between them. The unrecorded cost cannot change C's seat shortfall.

answer_basis.logical_reason: C is ineligible at every non-negative cost because its known seat count fails the minimum. A's higher seat count beats B among eligible plans.

tasks.misleading_error: Treats an unknown cost as decisive despite the known seat shortfall and invokes a tie rule when the remaining eligible seats differ.
tasks.explanation_anchor: C already fails the seat minimum, so its unknown cost cannot change eligibility. A and B qualify, and A's 24 seats exceed B's 22. A guessed cost is not needed.
tasks.development_concern: An irrelevant missing-cost case reverses the Y12 field-type shortcut. Matched A/B figures, C position, target wording, extra rule burden and misleading-advice plausibility remain untested.

tasks.learning_skill: Apply a supplied eligibility and ranking rule while distinguishing decisive from irrelevant missing information
tasks.title: School poetry event plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints
requirements.tie_break: Lower cost when seat counts tie

record.note: A's seat count was not recorded. All costs and seat counts are non-negative whole numbers; an unknown value is not zero. If eligible plans have the same seat count, choose the lower-cost plan.

tasks.claim: Plan C is the plan to choose under the stated rule.
tasks.shared_feedback: Not enough information. If A has 10 seats, it fails the minimum and C wins with 18 seats. If A has 22 seats, A qualifies and wins. At 18 seats, A wins the tie because 68 is less than C's cost of 74. These are possible completions, not observed counts; C's known seat count does not settle whether C is the choice.

answer_basis.logical_reason: Compatible values of A's missing seats can preserve or overturn C's selection. At equal seats, the explicit lower-cost rule selects A.

tasks.explanation_anchor: A's unreported seats can change eligibility or the ranking against C. Both a C-winning and an A-winning completion fit the record. The tie rule resolves equal seats but cannot supply the missing count; numerical examples are optional.
tasks.development_concern: New figures, context, row order and target differ from practice, but this is near transfer under the same rule. Missing seats, item position, claim target and label may remain cues; no age or difficulty equivalence established.

tasks.learning_skill: Apply a supplied eligibility and ranking rule while distinguishing decisive from irrelevant missing information
tasks.title: School craft demonstration plans

requirements.priority: Largest seat count among plans meeting both constraints
requirements.tie_break: Lower cost when seat counts tie

record.note: C's cost was not recorded. All costs and seat counts are non-negative whole numbers; an unknown value is not zero. If eligible plans have the same seat count, choose the lower-cost plan.

tasks.claim: Plan A is the plan to choose under the stated rule.
tasks.shared_feedback: Contradicted. C has 10 seats, below the minimum of 12, at every possible cost. A and B both qualify, but B has 20 seats and A has 16. B is the choice, so the claim about A is contradicted. A costs less, but lower cost is a tie rule, and their seat counts do not tie.

answer_basis.logical_reason: C's known seat shortfall excludes it at every non-negative cost. B beats A on eligible seats; lower cost cannot displace the primary priority when seats differ.

tasks.explanation_anchor: C cannot qualify because it has fewer than 12 seats, whatever its cost. B and A qualify; B has more seats, so A is not the choice. Mentioning only C's exclusion is incomplete because the claim concerns A versus B.
tasks.development_concern: An irrelevant omission yields Contradicted rather than Supported. Within these two new items, missing field and answer label are still correlated. This is not a matched factorial set or evidence that a shortcut has been eliminated.
